items.title: Newly Pending Listings Fell 17% In October, The Biggest Year Over Year Drop Since 2023 (Zillow October Market Report)
items.description: Newly Pending Listings Fell 17% In October, The Biggest Year Over Year Drop Since 2023 (Zillow October Market Report) Completed existing home sales fell 9% annually, according to Zillow’s preliminary sales nowcast. Written by Mischa Fisher on November 5, 2026 Key findings: Zillow’s preliminary measure of existing home sales fell 8.7% year over year in October. Newly pending listings — a leading indicator of next month’s closed sales — fell 16.8% year over year, the biggest decrease since August 2023. The typical mortgage payment in October was 12.8% higher than a year ago, according to Zillow’s estimates. The Zillow Observed Rent Index rose 2.9% year over year in October as the rental market continues to strengthen. The acute sting of suddenly higher mortgage rates is having the unfortunate effect on the housing market that last month’s pending sales data foretold. As mortgage rates entrenched themselves above 7%, home sales slowed sharply in October. Existing home sales fell 8.7% year over year, though that largely reflects sales agreed to in September, when mortgage rates were below 7% for much of the month. Newly pending listings, a leading indicator for the next month’s closed sales, fell 16.8% from last October, marking the biggest annual dip since August 2023 and slowest October since 2018. November is shaping up to have an even larger contraction in sales activity, but the silver lining is that next month is likely going to be the worst of it. The pace of the slowdown is expected to ease into the new year. A jump in housing costs likely drove the slowdown. The monthly mortgage payment on the typical U.S. home was an estimated $2,004 in October, assuming a 20% down payment and excluding taxes and insurance. That’s up 12.8% from last year and 4.8% higher than in September, the biggest one-month jump in four years. For a buyer putting only 5% down and securing an FHA loan, which comes with a lower mortgage rate, the year-over-year rise has been similar at 11.8%. Once insurance, taxes and maintenance are factored in, a median-income household would spend 41.5% of its income on that monthly payment, up from 39.2% a year ago. The rise in mortgage costs is almost exclusively due to higher mortgage rates. The typical U.S. home value fell 0.6% month over month and is just 0.7% higher than a year earlier, as measured by the Zillow Home Value Index. Meanwhile, mortgage rates averaged 7.33% in October, according to Freddie Mac , up from 6.86% in September. As for-sale activity wanes, the rental market continues to strengthen. The typical U.S. rent is up 2.9% year over year, according to the Zillow Observed Rent Index. That’s the strongest annual gain in the past 19 months, and marks the seventh consecutive month that annual rent growth has increased. While there is no avoiding that this has been a very soft fall for for-sale activity, there are deals to be had for buyers able to brave the affordability headwinds in the coming months. Buyers usually have leverage this time of year when sellers try to make a deal before the holidays, and especially so this year given current market conditions. The continued inventory buildup means there is a lot of upside for sales into next year if we get rate relief. More data, including dashboards with local market data , can be found on the refreshed Zillow Research website . The Zillow November Market Report is expected to be released December 4 . Home Values & Mortgage Payments The typical U.S. home value is $364,812, according to the Zillow Home Value Index (ZHVI). ZHVI fell 0.6% month over month in October. Home values are 0.7% higher than a year earlier. The monthly mortgage payment on a typical U.S. home is $2,004, assuming a 20% down payment and excluding taxes and insurance. That is 12.8% higher than last year. Inventory There were 1.4 million homes for sale nationwide in October. Active inventory was 3.4% higher than a year earlier. Inventory rose 0.4% from September. New for-sale listings totaled 328,328 in October, down 4.2% from a year earlier and down 4.4% from September. Sales 304,105 homes were sold in October, according to the preliminary Zillow sales count nowcast. That is 8.7% lower than a year earlier and down 5.4% from September. These figures will be revised mid-month. Newly pending listings, which measures listings that changed from for-sale to pending status rather than closed sales, shows a 16.8% decrease from a year earlier and a 9.1% decrease over September. Affordability A household earning the median income would need to spend 34.7% of its income on the typical monthly mortgage payment (assuming a typically valued home and a 20% down payment, and including estimates for taxes, maintenance and insurance). That is up from 32.7% a year earlier and up from 33.5% in September. A household earning the median income would need to spend 26% of its income on the typical rent in October. That is unchanged from a year earlier and from September. Competition Homes took a median of 31 days to go pending in October. That was two days longer than a year earlier and two days longer than September. The share of listings with a price cut in October was 26.5%. That was down from 26.9% a year earlier and down from 27.3% in September. 25.6% of homes sold above list price in September, the most recent data available. That’s compared to 25.2% a year earlier and 27.5% in August. Rents The typical rent nationwide is $1,913, according to the Zillow Observed Rent Index. That’s 2.9% higher than a year earlier and flat from September. 40.4% of rental listings on Zillow offered a concession in October. That’s up from 38.7% a year earlier and up from 39.6% in September. items.title: Multifamily Developer Confidence Weakens in Third Quarter
items.description: Multifamily Developer Confidence Weakens in Third Quarter November 5, 2026 Eric Lynch No Comments New multifamily housing confidence weakened year-over-year in the third quarter, according to the Multifamily Market Survey (MMS) by the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB). The MMS produces two separate indices. The Multifamily Production Index (MPI) had a reading of 41, down five points year-over-year, while the Multifamily Occupancy Index (MOI) had a reading of 69, also down five points year-over-year. Developer sentiment for new multifamily production has softened, due to challenges such as high interest rates , construction costs that are high relative to rents, and problems getting projects approved and connected to roads and utilities, resulting in many projects taking longer to complete. Due to the headwinds facing the industry, NAHB’s 2027 forecast shows a decline for multifamily starts. Although the administration’s regulatory reform efforts are helping to ease some cost pressures, the multifamily sector would still benefit from an expedited permit process and lower rates on development and construction loans . Multifamily Production Index (MPI) The MMS asks multifamily developers to rate the current conditions as “good ”, “fair”, or “poor” for multifamily starts in markets where they are active. The index and all its components are scaled so that a number above 50 indicates that more respondents report conditions as good rather than poor. The MPI is a weighted average of four key market segments: three in the built-for-rent market (garden/low-rise, mid/high-rise, and subsidized) and the built-for-sale (or condominium) market. All four components experienced decreases year-over-year and are in negative territory (i.e., below 50) during the third quarter. The component measuring subsidized units fell six points to 49, the component measuring garden/low-rise dropped five points to 48, and both the component measuring mid/high-rise units and the component measuring built-for-sale units decreased four points to 33 and 31, respectively. Multifamily Occupancy Index (MOI) The survey also asks multifamily property owners to rate the current conditions for occupancy of existing rental apartments in markets where they are active as “good”, “fair”, or “poor”. Like the MPI, the MOI and all its components are scaled so that a number above 50 indicates more respondents report that occupancy is good than poor. The MOI is a weighted average of three built-for-rent market segments (garden/low-rise, mid/high-rise, and subsidized). Two of the three components experienced declines year-over-year for the third quarter of 2026. The mid/high-rise component declined seven points to 59 and the garden/low-rise component fell six points to 70. The component measuring subsidized units saw an increase of two points to 83. Nevertheless, all three components remained above the break-even point of 50. Changes in Overall Market Conditions The MMS was re-designed in 2023 to produce results that are easier to interpret and consistent with the proven format of other NAHB industry sentiment surveys. Until there is enough data to seasonally adjust the series, changes in the MMS indices should only be evaluated on a year-over-year basis. For more recent information about the market, the survey contains a separate question asking multifamily developers to compare current market conditions to conditions three months earlier. In the third quarter of 2026, 6% of respondents said the current market is better, and 28% said it is worse. However, the majority of developers—66%—said that the market is currently about the same as it was three months ago. Please visit NAHB’s MMS web page for the full report. items.title: CFPB narrows enforcement practices, closes 86% of supervisory actions
items.description: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau ( CFPB ) said that it is narrowing its supervisory and enforcement activities and closing most of its outstanding supervisory actions, as well as pursuing changes to mortgage lending and servicing rules, according to its latest semi-annual report, released Oct. 27. The report, which covers the first half of 2026, outlines the bureau’s efforts to align its work with the Trump administration ’s priorities. During the broader reporting period of July 2025 through June 2026, the CFPB closed 1,327 of the 1,552 supervisory actions that were open as of July 1, 2025, or approximately 86%. The bureau said the closures reflected either institutions sufficiently addressing the issues or findings that no longer aligned with its priorities. The CFPB also reassessed all 80 open examinations and closed 66 that did not align with its revised priorities. The remaining 14 continued with a focus on correcting violations, addressing compliance weaknesses and providing relief to affected consumers. The bureau also reduced the number of scheduled examinations by approximately 50%, shifting its attention toward depository institutions , activities it deemed actual consumer fraud and areas within its statutory authority. Mortgage origination and servicing remain among its supervisory priorities. Under its new approach, the CFPB said examinations will focus on clearly identified products and potential violations tied to specific laws and regulations. The bureau also plans to avoid duplicating oversight already conducted by state or other federal regulators. Mortgage rules under review The CFPB is pursuing several mortgage-related regulatory changes under President Donald Trump’s executive order on promoting access to mortgage credit. Among its priorities is a review of the ability-to-repay requirements and qualified mortgage definitions under Regulation Z. The bureau is evaluating whether to modify the requirements, which apply to most residential mortgages. The CFPB is also considering a final rule to streamline mortgage servicing requirements under Regulation X. The proposal, initially issued in July 2024, is intended to simplify the loss-mitigation review process and make it easier for servicers to assist borrowers who experience payment difficulties. In July 2026, after the report’s primary reporting period, the bureau also issued a request for information seeking feedback on ways to promote access to mortgage credit. The CFPB additionally finalized changes to its fair lending and small-business lending rules. In April, the bureau amended Regulation B, which implements the Equal Credit Opportunity Act. The rule removed longstanding language supporting disparate-impact liability and revised restrictions on discouraging prospective credit applicants. It also prohibited for-profit creditors from using race, color, national origin or sex as eligibility criteria for Special Purpose Credit Programs . A separate May rule revised requirements for small-business lending data collection under Section 1071 of the Dodd-Frank Act. Among other changes, it lowered the annual revenue threshold for businesses covered by the rule from $5 million to $1 million, removed certain data collection requirements and extended the compliance date to Jan. 1, 2028. Fair lending and enforcement The bureau said it did not cite any fair lending violations during the reporting period, and that while it continued investigations, it instead focused its efforts on cases involving intentional discrimination with identifiable victims. It also made no referrals to the Department of Justice for potential patterns or practices of lending discrimination. Overall, the CFPB said it closed approximately 40% of its pending investigations as part of its effort to align enforcement with its revised priorities. The bureau reported receiving approximately 8.27 million consumer complaints between July 1, 2025, and June 30, 2026. It sent approximately 7.5 million complaints to companies for review, and companies responded to 99.6% of those complaints. The report's complaint figures come as the CFPB has moved to limit the public availability of consumer complaints. In August, the bureau said it would stop publishing unverified complaint narratives and related data visualizations in its public database, arguing that the accounts present only one side of a dispute and may not reflect violations of law. The bureau also said it would continue collecting complaints, reviewing company responses and sharing information with regulators. Previously published narratives will remain available through its Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) reading room. items.title: US Apartment Rents Inch Higher in Q3 as Supply Wave Subsides
items.description: National CRE News In Your Inbox. Sign up for Connect emails to stay informed with CRE stories that are 150 words or less. National + Apartments | November 5, 2026 By: Greg Isaacson US Apartment Rents Inch Higher in Q3 as Supply Wave Subsides CBRE’s latest multifamily research shows an improvement in market fundamentals as U.S. apartment rents grew slightly in the third quarter and new construction continued to slow. Average apartment rents rose by 1% year-over-year and 0.5% quarter-over-quarter to $2,268, the brokerage found. Positive performance in across the Midwest, Northeast and Pacific regions supported rent growth, with San Francisco recording the largest year-over-year jump at 9.4%. Multifamily construction completions totaled 84,300 units during the quarter, falling 11% compared to the same quarter of 2025. However, completions outpaced net absorption for the first time since the fourth quarter of 2025, contributing to an increase in the overall vacancy rate by 40 basis points to 4.7%. Total net absorption in the third quarter was just 8,747 units, down from 42,166 a year ago, and CBRE expects absorption to continue to fall in the coming quarters as construction slows further. Investment volume in the sector soared 140% year-over-year to $112.3 billion in the third quarter, but the increase was mainly driven by the $69.6 billion merger of Avalon Bay and Equity Residential. “With peak supply now behind us and rent growth poised to strengthen, the sector is positioned for a gradual recovery in transaction activity,” noted Kelli Carhart, Head of Multifamily Capital Markets for CBRE in a statement. items.title: NAR: Repeat buyers dominate home sales as first-time buyers struggle to enter the market
items.description: NAR: Repeat buyers dominate home sales as first-time buyers struggle to enter the market by Jacqui Mueller November 05, 2026 Repeat buyers accounted for 78% of home purchases in 2026, while first-time buyers made up just 22%, showing the gap between repeat buyers and those buying their first home, according to the National Association of REALTORS® ' 2026 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers . The share of first-time buyers rose slightly from 21% in last year's report, which was a record low, but remains well below the historical norm of 40% before 2008. Their median age remained 40, the highest on record. Repeat buyers had a median age of 62, tying the previous record. That gap was also clear in how buyers paid for their homes. Thirty percent of repeat buyers purchased with cash, while their median down payment was 19%. First-time buyers made a median down payment of 9%, and 10% purchased with cash, the highest share recorded for that group. Among first-time buyers who paid all cash, 28% used an inheritance. That compares with 9% of first-time buyers who financed their purchases. The median age of first-time all-cash buyers was 54, compared with 38 for those who financed. Repeat buyers also had a median household income of $127,000, up from $111,700 in the previous report. Fifty-seven percent used proceeds from the sale of their previous home for a down payment. First-time buyers relied most heavily on personal savings, with 62% using that source. Thirty percent used financial assets such as retirement accounts, stocks or cryptocurrency, while 25% used gifts or loans from family and friends. Ten percent used an inheritance for a down payment, the highest share recorded. Financial assets have now accounted for a larger share of first-time buyer down payment sources than gifts or loans for two consecutive years. Saving for a down payment remained a major obstacle. Twenty-eight percent of first-time buyers identified it as the most difficult step in the buying process, compared with 6% of repeat buyers. Among buyers who had difficulty saving, 50% cited high rent or an existing mortgage payment. Credit card debt was cited by 35%, student loans by 32% and car loans by 31%. The financial sacrifices made to buy a home also differed between the two groups. Sixty-two percent of first-time buyers said they made sacrifices to save for a down payment, compared with 31% of repeat buyers. Buyers said they cut back on nonessential purchases, entertainment and clothing, and some canceled vacation plans. The report also found that 29% of first-time buyers carried student loan debt, compared with 10% of repeat buyers. The median student loan debt among buyers with those loans was $35,000. How buyers are approaching homeownership The profile of buyers is changing in other ways, too. Four percent of buyers purchased with unromantic roommates, an all-time high. Among first-time buyers, that share was 5%. Fourteen percent bought multigenerational homes, often to care for aging parents (30%) or save money (23%). The desire to own a home remained the leading reason for first-time buyers (60%) to make a purchase. Among repeat buyers, 18% said they wanted to be closer to family and friends, while 13% wanted a larger home. Finding the right property remained a challenge for buyers. Fifty-six percent identified it as the most difficult step in the homebuying process. For first-time buyers (39%), understanding the steps involved in purchasing a home was the biggest challenge. Buyers spent a median of 10 weeks searching for a home. Forty-six percent began the process by looking online for properties, while 19% contacted a real estate agent first. Overall, 53% found the home they purchased on the internet, 28% through an agent and 8% through a friend, relative or neighbor. The role of real estate agents Despite the challenges facing buyers, real estate professionals continued to play a central role in transactions. Ninety percent of buyers used an agent or broker, the highest share recorded. That figure rose to 93% among buyers of previously owned homes. Finding the right home was the service buyers most wanted from their agents (51%). Another 15% prioritized help negotiating the terms of a sale, while 12% wanted help with price negotiations. Agents also helped buyers navigate the process and evaluate properties. Fifty-five percent said their agent pointed out features or faults they had not noticed, and 54% said their agent helped them understand the homebuying process. This was especially important for first-time buyers, with 78% saying their agent helped them understand the process, compared with 47% of repeat buyers. Most buyers still found their agent through personal connections. Forty percent found their agent through a friend, neighbor or relative, while 23% worked with an agent they had previously used. Among first-time buyers, 52% found their agent through a personal referral. Just 1% of buyers found their agent through an AI search. Sellers also continued to rely on real estate professionals. Ninety-two percent used an agent or broker, a record high, while for-sale-by-owner transactions accounted for 5% of sales, matching the all-time low. Homeowners stayed in their properties for a median of 12 years before selling, the longest period recorded in the report. That was twice the six-year median recorded between 2000 and 2008. Moving closer to friends and family was the leading reason for selling, cited by 22% of sellers. When choosing a listing agent, sellers (31%) placed the greatest importance on the agent's reputation. Another 24% identified honesty and trustworthiness as the most important factor. Sellers most often wanted help marketing their homes and setting a competitive price (20%). items.description: Small businesses feel the squeeze Commercial and industrial lending to large and middle-market firms was broadly unchanged from the previous survey — but banks tightened lending to smaller businesses. "Banks reported tightening standards for premiums charged on riskier loans for firms of all sizes," the report noted. Lenders pointed to a less favorable or more uncertain economic outlook, and a worsening of industry-specific problems as the key reason for the shift. U.S. 10-Year Treasurys. Commercial real estate is also emerging as a pressure point, with banks reporting tightened standards across the board on construction and land development, nonfarm nonresidential properties, and multifamily properties, and weakening demand for loans in all CRE categories. U.S. banks are also tightening credit standards for nonbank financial firms such as private equity funds and business and mortgage credit intermediaries. items.title: MORE HOUSTON HOUSEHOLDS ABLE TO AFFORD A HOME AS PRICES EASE
items.description: MORE HOUSTON HOUSEHOLDS ABLE TO AFFORD A HOME AS PRICES EASE 42% of Houston-area households were able to buy a home in the third quarter HOUSTON -- (November 5, 2026) -- More Houston-area households were able to buy a home in the third quarter as home prices eased, according to the latest Housing and Rental Affordability Report from the Houston Association of Realtors. HAR's Housing Affordability Index shows that 42% of households in the Greater Houston area could afford a median-priced home, up from 39% in the third quarter of 2025. The median home price declined 0.4% year over year to $340,300 from $341,600 the prior year. The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate was 6.68%, compared with 6.57% during the same quarter last year. The typical monthly mortgage payment, including principal, taxes and insurance, was $2,520, compared with $2,510 in Q3 2025. Households needed a minimum annual income of $100,800 to purchase the median-priced home, which is flat from a year earlier. "Affordability is moving in the right direction, and that's encouraging, but we also know many consumers are still concerned about the cost of buying a home, particularly with mortgage rates remaining elevated," said HAR Chair Theresa Hill with Compass RE Texas, LLC -- Houston. "For buyers who may have been sitting on the sidelines, it's worth taking another look at what's possible. A Realtor can help buyers understand their options and determine what's realistic for their budget." Across Texas, 45% of households could afford a median-priced home in the third quarter, compared with 42% last year. The statewide median home price declined to $335,000 from $337,500, while the minimum annual income needed to purchase the median-priced home held at $92,400. Nationally, 38% of households could afford a median-priced home, up from 35% in 2025. According to the National Association of Realtors, the U.S. median home price increased to $432,900 from $426,800. The minimum qualifying income rose to $112,000 from $109,200. The chart below shows how the minimum annual household income needed to purchase a home has changed year-over-year. Rental Affordability Update Forty-four percent of Houston-area households could afford the median monthly lease payment in the third quarter of 2026, according to HAR's Rental Affordability Index. That is down from 45% in 2025. The median monthly lease was $2,195 compared with $2,200 a year earlier. A household needed a minimum annual income of $87,800 to qualify for the median lease payment, compared with $88,000 the prior year. The chart below shows how the median lease price for a single-family home has changed year-over-year. items.title: Florida’s Amendment 3 could give housing market a ‘sugar high’ through year-end
items.description: Jason Haber, a Compass broker licensed in both Florida and New York, believes the Sunshine State’s approval of Amendment 3 will lead to the state’s housing market experiencing a “sugar high” to close out the year. Amendment 3 , which was approved by 62% of the electorate on Tuesday, easily surpassing the 60% threshold, increases the homestead exemption, reducing the taxable value of a person's primary residence in the state. Prior to this, homeowners could receive an exemption of up to $50,000, but the amendment increases the exemption on non-school property taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. Beyond that, the amendment says the exemption will be adjusted for inflation. This means that if someone's primary residence has an assessed value of $350,000, in 2028, the new $250,000 exemption would leave $100,000 subject to non-school property taxes, assuming the homeowner qualifies for the full exemption, generating potentially thousands of dollars in savings for homeowners. Haber agrees that the amendment could create “serious property tax savings for those who homestead in Florida.” “That was clearly very attractive to the majority of people. Affordability is the top domestic issue of our time right now and people see this as direct relief on their cost of living,” Haber said. Carrots to entice people to move to the Sunshine State But the amendment comes with a caveat. Homeowners must establish primary residency in Florida before Dec. 31, 2026, in order to be eligible for the 2027 and 2028 exemptions. If you establish primary residency after the deadline, you will have to wait five years until you're eligible for the expanded exemptions, which is why Haber believes the market may experience a “sugar high.” “If you were on the fence this would certainly move you to act quickly,” Haber said, noting that Florida uses a variety of “carrots” to entice people to move to the state. Chris Wands, the founder of The Wands Team , a RealTrends Verified ranked team, at Douglas Elliman , a RealTrends Verified brokerage, shares a similar view. “It may make people move faster especially if they are already planning to move in the first half of next year,” Wands said. “I think it makes Florida an even more attractive state. A lot of people are moving here for the tax benefits, so adding another benefit helps with that.” If a “sugar high” market does happen, local real estate professionals said it could have greater impacts on some markets than others. “In Boca Raton right now, if a house is priced properly, you will have six people fighting over it, but that isn’t the case in every market. Further north in the state, the market is weaker because those markets are more impacted by high interest rates, so it would be a different story there," Haber said. Danielle Blake, the chief of residential and advocacy at Miami Realtors + RWorld , shares a similar view. “Availability of inventory is going to vary by the asset class that you are looking for, whether it is single family or condominiums, and also the geographic location. In Miami, we have more condo inventory than single-family inventory at affordable price points, but that also varies by cities. Some cities have a larger supply, so it really varies,” Blake said. In addition to a potential uptick in new residents, Wands also believes this could impact current primary residents’ decisions on purchasing larger properties, especially if they were previously concerned about how property taxes could impact their long-term affordability. This could then open up more mid-level or entry-level properties, helping more people get into the housing market. Blake however, is skeptical, noting that despite this impacting the property tax portion of the affordability equation, many current homeowners may be reluctant to give up the 3% mortgage rate they have on their current property, especially in today’s mortgage rate environment. In addition to this, property taxes in Florida are reset when a property is sold, meaning that if the purchase price goes up, so do the property taxes. “Even if you're not paying as much as you otherwise would have, anything that pushes up purchase price and, by extension, property taxes can have that adverse impact on affordability,” Haber said. Additionally, legislators could increase the millage rate, which would hamper the affordability benefits homeowners are hoping to gain out of this amendment. items.title: Opportunity Zone Home Price Growth Largely Tracks Other Areas
items.description: Opportunity Zone Home Price Growth Largely Tracks Other Areas by ATTOM Team | Nov 5, 2026 | Home Sales & Prices , Real Estate News - Recent Articles Median home prices grew year-over-year in 48.9 percent of Opportunity Zone census tracts, compared to 51.6 percent of tracts outside the zones. IRVINE, Cal. — Nov. 5, 2026 — ATTOM , the leading provider of property data , AI-powered intelligence , and real estate analytics solutions, today released its third-quarter 2026 report analyzing qualified low-income Opportunity Zones targeted by Congress for economic redevelopment in the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 (see full methodology below). In this report, ATTOM looked at 3,805 census tracts in Opportunity Zones around the United States with sufficient data to analyze, meaning they had at least five home sales in the third quarter of the year. Median single-family home and condo prices rose quarter-over-quarter in 48.1 percent (1,651) of the 3,431 Opportunity Zone tracts with sufficient data in both the second and third quarter. Year-over-year, home prices rose in 48.9 percent (1,598) of the 3,265 tracts with sufficient data in the third quarters of 2025 and 2026. Typical home prices rose year-over-year in 51.6 percent (28,212) of the 54,704 census tracts outside of Opportunity Zones with sufficient data in both quarters to be included in the analysis, meaning that price growth was more common outside the targeted economic development zones than inside them. In 9.4 percent (357) of Opportunity Zone census tracts, the third quarter of 2026 marked the highest median home value since the beginning of the Great Recession in 2008 and 27.1 percent of the Opportunity Zone census tracts experienced double-digit growth in home values year-over-year. “Opportunity Zones remain a notably lower-cost segment of the housing market, with nearly 80 percent of these areas posting median home prices below the national median,” said Rob Barber, CEO of ATTOM. “Even so , home values were only slightly less likely to rise in these areas in the third quarter, suggesting that many of these communities are still moving broadly with the market.” The national median home sales price in the third quarter was $368,000. Inside Opportunity Zones, 79.5 percent of census tracts in ATTOM’s analysis had typical home prices below the national median. Outside the zones, only 50.4 percent of census tracts in the analysis had typical prices below the national median. Due to the small number of sales in many Opportunity Zone census tracts, median price measurements can be volatile. The typical median sales price rose or fell by more than 5 percent quarter-over-quarter in 79.1 percent of the 3,431 tracts with sufficient data in the second and third quarters. Outside the zones, 29.4 percent of included tracts experienced at least double-digit growth. Among states with at least 25 Opportunity Zone census tracts with sufficient data to analyze, Maine had the largest share that experienced year-over-year median home price growth (64 percent), followed by South Carolina (61.3 percent), Wisconsin (58.3 percent), Virginia (53 percent), and Oregon (52.3 percent). Statistics for previous quarters are revised when each new report is issued as more deed data becomes available. items.title: Ellington eyes non-QM servicing growth in new acquisition
items.description: Ellington eyes non-QM servicing growth in new acquisition By Spencer Lee CloseText About Spencer twitter Spencer_NYC linkedin spencer-lee-journo Published November 05, 2026, 2:56 p.m. EST | Updated November 05, 2026, 3:52 p.m. EST 3 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Ellington Financial believes its new servicer acquisition presents it with opportunity to stand out in the specialized, growing segments it operates in and holds potential to attract future customers also active in the space. Processing Content The real estate investment trust announced its purchase this week of Statebridge Co., a diversified loan servicer, whose expertise primarily covers late-stage distress, along with residential-transition and other non-qualified mortgages . The move points to the diversification strategy occurring across mortgage businesses of all types, in response to changing expectations in origination mix and borrower performance over the coming months. The decision to acquire a servicer came about, in part, from industry contraction, which made it challenging for Ellington to find a partner that could effectively work with the types of delinquent and non-QM loans it owns. The company hinted at the likely merger over the summer in its second-quarter earnings. "We didn't see great options where we could really get what we think are best-in-class protocols, and have a dialog and be able to use our data analysis and our kind of native experience and expertise in the product to effectuate outcomes," said Ellington Co-Chief Investment Officer Mark Tecotzky on Thursday in its latest earnings call. While leaders advised that financial benefits might not appear on the balance sheet immediately, the upside would come in the longer term. "We're going to build this into the premier special servicer," added CEO Larry Penn. "Even with what we see as the delinquency pipeline now, once we've built this, I think there'll be plenty of business for Statebridge to grow and thrive on." As of September 30, Statebridge serviced approximately 14,700 loans representing an approximate unpaid principal balance of $1.9 billion, nearly all for third-party clients. The portfolio includes 3,500 non-QM and RTL loans, with balances totaling $1.1 billion, as well as a smaller subset of agency and commercial mortgages. With the attention now paid to the non-QM segment, the need to understand the nuances of those particular types of loans will also give Statebridge an advantage, Tecotzky explained. "Delinquencies when non-QM first started were trivially small," he said, noting the effect of Covid-era home-price appreciation on the housing market. "We don't see that HPA tailwind right now obviously, so we think long-term delinquencies will tick up to levels that are more consistent with reasonable expectations." "As we build this out, and we demonstrate the quality of the resolutions we believe Statebridge can get, others may want to use their services," Tecotzky continued. Ellington and Longbridge post "solid" third quarter The acquisition came in a third quarter when Ellington reported net income of $45.9 million, which represented a 20.9% decrease from the prior three-month period's $58 million. On a year-over-year basis, profit climbed 21.6% from $37.8 million. The bottom line numbers factored in results across its businesses, including its investment portfolio and reverse lending unit, Longbridge Financial, as well as changes in fair market value. "This was a solid quarter for EFC, against a market backdrop that has a lot more landmines than in the first half of the year," Tecotzky said. The portfolio investment arm was able to price two non-QM securitizations and a single agency-eligible transaction early in the quarter before spreads widened, he noted. With increased interest in non-QM and non-agency loans, the pace of such deals is approaching $5 billion a week, Ellington officials also noted. Interest rate pressures, though, led the company to introduce a sequential pay structure to address investor concerns about reduced refinance incentive. "Other non-QM issuers quickly adopted that approach," Tecotzky said. Net income at the Longbridge subsidiary came in at $12.5 million, 58.8% below the second-quarter's $30.2 million. Compared to a year ago, the reverse-lending business increased its profit by 4.5% from $8.6 million. Longbridge celebrated originations of $676.3 million during the third quarter, with volume rising 36% from the same three months in 2025. From July to September, the company grew its share of government-backed Home Equity Conversion Mortgage transactions to a record 31%, making it the second-largest issuer in the market. Meanwhile, among its proprietary offerings , September proved to be the strongest month ever for the products. "If anything, we're hoping for and expecting continued growth into next year," Penn said. "We do see the product continues to gain traction. Demographics are favorable, and I think the product makes a lot of sense. Obviously, we're broadening the product base as well." items.title: Democrats Eye Tougher Data Center Regulations as They Regain Control of Congress
items.description: Democrats who rode data center discontent to victory in the midterms are expected to pursue strict new regulations on data centers when they take control of Congress in January. The Democratic sweep flipped dozens of House and Senate seats, and a number of those races hinged on broadsides against Republicans for their purported support of the industry. Meanwhile, voters considered more than 40 local measures to constrain data center development, and almost all of them passed. The results are likely to bring new life into Democrats' efforts to add guardrails to the artificial intelligence buildout. But their majority does not go far enough to override a veto from President Donald Trump , who has sought to aggressively promote data centers in the United States, in the pursuit of what he dubs "super intelligence." Polls show broad concerns that the pace of data center construction could drive up power costs , raise land prices, and create environmental problems. Recent Realtor.com® research on data centers found they're increasingly moving into rural areas. "If the Democrats take control of Congress, it could be a major problem for data center developers," Balaji Tammabattula , CEO of BaRupOn LLC, which develops energy infrastructure for data center companies, recently told Realtor.com. Data center companies, he said, are already reconsidering future investments. In Texas , Senate winner James Talarico released a blueprint for data center regulation with more enforcement. The state has a temporary moratorium on data centers in place, which Democratic Gov.-Elect Gina Hinojosa has pledged to extend. Just a few hours before polls closed, The Hill reported that Microsoft, Amazon, Meta, Google, and other tech companies were considering a more formal framework for data center development. "Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Elon Musk posted on X shortly after the results came in. What's on the table Congress' one effort to rein in the impacts of data centers fell short just before the midterms. Several weeks ago, the House passed a bill to encourage utilities to shield ratepayers from the costs associated with data center buildouts, the Ratepayer Protection Act . That followed widespread backlash against data center buildouts . But Senate Democrats tanked the bill because it didn't go far enough. They've coalesced around a few competing ideas for how to regulate data centers at the federal level. In the meantime, Democrats put forth their own bill, the Guaranteeing Rate Insulation from Data Centers (GRID) Act , with more enforcement power and penalties. Among its powers, it would require data center developers to provide their own energy, so they don't pull from the local power grid. It would also require more disclosure about data center developments and give the government the power to issue fines. Also, 20 Democrats signed on to a bill that would create a total moratorium on data center development. But the president has veto power, and he has opposed such a harsh move. Trump has advocated for data center development in the United States to prevent the technology being developed abroad. In the face of public backlash, he convened technology leaders in Washington in September and asked them to self-police the build-out of super intelligence. The White House also released an accord signed by those major companies committing to developing the technology safely. Trump called it "morally binding." Loading... Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei leaves the U.S. Capitol surrounded by aides and security after meeting with President Donald Trump on Sept. 29. Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images What it means locally While data centers affect property taxes , the exact impact on homeowners' tax burden is complicated. And the study found no impact on property values from large facilities in the two years after they open. Democrats may find an opening to create more rules around data center construction. Although Democrats also took control of governor's offices in many major states with data center developments, Realtor.com senior economist Jake Krimmel says that doesn't necessarily mean they will lead to sharp constraints on data centers. "Utilities costs, rather than home values, are probably the biggest immediate change voters are feeling or fearing," Krimmel says. "Our analysis of data center impacts on the housing market found essentially no effect on inventory or sales behavior so far." The Urban Institute suggested a few levers to help data centers support housing affordability. It suggested tax relief or energy cost offsets for communities that host many data centers. Otherwise, they risk straining local housing markets due to rising electricity costs, especially in high-growth regions. Meanwhile, Brookings suggested an electricity tax on data centers or some kind of offset to local governments. But it warned that regulation of the sector could encourage developers to build more centers overseas. It's unlikely the currently divided Congress will use the remainder of its term to pass rules around data centers. But when the new one comes in, it can reintroduce the GRID Act or other bills. The GRID Act’s 20-megawatt threshold would cover essentially the entire pipeline, more than 99% of planned capacity, Krimmel says. "That would give homeowners the most direct protection on rates," Krimmel explains. "Requiring new projects to bring their own power could also slow data center development, and the jury is also still out on the local economic and labor market impacts of data centers on localities." items.title: Safest and riskiest places to live in the U.S. 2050
items.description: Safety has a price, and it will be paid. Cotality analyzed the top 10 safest and riskiest places to live in the U.S. and found that the areas or the country that are least vulnerable to natural catastrophes are also where prices are growing the fastest. In all states, the cost of homeownership is no longer calculated by mortgage payments alone. As the risk of natural disasters increases, insuring a home is increasingly determining the final monthly cost of being a homeowner. At the same time, people are paying more to live in regions where natural catastrophes are of less concern. Pennsylvania recorded some of the most pronounced year-over-year home price growth in August 2026. Arizona and the District of Columbia are poised to see the most price growth in the coming year, according to Cotality’s Home Price Index. These states will also be some of the safest come 2050. items.title: Simon Property Group Takes Out $93M Loan To Refinance Colorado Mills Mall
items.description: Wikimedia Commons/Jeffrey Beall Simon Property Group took out a $93M loan for Lakewood’s Colorado Mills mall, with $80M being sold into CMBS , according to a term sheet filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday. The loan, granted by Goldman Sachs and German American Capital Corp. , has an interest rate of approximately 6.84%. It is set to mature in November 2036, according to the SEC filing. Simon didn’t respond to multiple requests for comment from Bisnow . Colorado Mills is one of the largest shopping centers in the Denver metro. The 1.4M SF mall was built in 2002 and renovated after a ferocious 2017 hailstorm that seriously damaged the property and led to its temporary closure. It was 98% occupied as of Aug. 31, according to the SEC filing. The mall added Cavender’s Boot City as a new tenant earlier this month. In early 2025, Colorado Mills was reappraised at $135M, 37% less than its 2014 valuation. Simon took out a $117.7M loan in 2014 that was transferred to special servicing before its November 2024 maturity date, Bisnow previously reported . In May 2025, after the property was reappraised, Simon avoided default on the loan by securing a two-year extension deal . Colorado Mills’ net operating income has fluctuated over the years, but the property appears to be performing better this year. Its net operating income through the first seven months of 2026 was about $18.7M, up nearly $1.3M from last year, according to the SEC filing. Colorado Mills’ $80M CMBS loan is part of an $805M pool with 63 commercial mortgage loans backed by 79 properties across the U.S. The local mall’s loan is the largest in the pool, accounting for about 10%, Kroll Bond Rating Agency said in a statement. Malls across the country have faced shifting market conditions over the past decade. The number of malls in the U.S. dropped from 2,500 in the 1980s to 700 in 2024. Despite the closures, malls are now the “top performer in commercial real estate,” with values increasing 13% year-over-year, The Wall Street Journal reported . Park Meadows mall in Lone Tree also faced a potential default in 2024. The mall’s owner, Brookfield Properties, refinanced by securing a $700M loan with a five-year term just days before its previous $615M property loan matured. items.description: Homebuyers Get Some Relief as Prices Decline For Third Straight Week, Monthly Payments Dip Published on November 5th, 2026 by Dana Anderson New listings of homes for sale fell to their lowest level since the start of the year, but there are still significantly more sellers than buyers in the market. What to know about the U.S. housing market for the four weeks ending November 1: Prices fell for the third week in a row. The median home-sale price was $388,604, down 0.4% year over year. That marks the third straight week in which prices declined after three years of increases. Monthly payments dropped to a 5-week low. The median monthly mortgage payment was $2,777, down from a peak of $2,811 in early October. This data is seasonally adjusted. Costs declined because mortgage rates and sale prices are slowly coming down. House hunting activity declined. Pending home sales fell 0.6% week over week to the lowest level in records dating back to 2021. Sellers pulled back, too. New listings dropped 1.5% from a week earlier to the lowest level since January, as would-be sellers reacted to slow demand. The slow market is giving buyers room to negotiate. The buyers who are out there may be able to negotiate prices down and/or get other concessions from sellers. Buyers have more homes to choose from than a year ago, and less competition: There are 2.1% more homes on the market than a year ago, while homes are taking a bit longer to sell. items.title: Absolute Home Mortgage, First Option leaders on strengthening their partnership
items.description: On Wednesday, Absolute Home Mortgage Corp. and First Option Mortgage announced a strategic transaction that combines the companies' resources and aims for originations growth amid a consolidating market . Matthew VanFossen , the CEO of New Jersey-based Absolute, and Alvin Shah, managing partner at Georgia-based First Option, sat down with HousingWire shortly after the announcement to offer further details. The deal, which combines the two companies with Mortgage Equity Partners — a wholly owned subsidiary of Absolute — is positioned to originate about $4 billion annually across roughly 420 producing loan officers. items.title: Jemal Equities Buys Carr Properties' Former HQ In Receivership Sale
items.description: One of the most active office buyers in D.C. has purchased yet another property in the center of the city. Jemal Equities, founded last year by Matthew Jemal , the son of Douglas Development head Douglas Jemal, paid $45M for the office building at 1615 L St. NW, D.C. deed records show. Google Maps The 417K SF office building at 1615 L St. NW in downtown Washington, D.C. The 417K SF property, which sits a block away from the Farragut North Metro station, was previously owned by Carr Properties but has been controlled by a receiver since 2024. A judge with the D.C. Superior Court approved the sale by the receiver in July, court records show. Two limited liability companies managed by Jemal, 1615 L FS LLC and Jemal's RI 1615 LLC, took out a $48M loan for the purchase from NEG Financing I LLC, deed records show, $45M of which was used for the acquisition. Jemal Equities and Carr Properties didn’t respond to requests for comment. The office building at 1615 L was 27.6% leased as of September, according to special servicer commentary filed in Morningstar Credit’ s database, down from 67.6% occupancy as of the end of 2024. The building lost a two-floor tenant in January 2025, a full-floor tenant that April, and another full-floor tenant that August, according to the servicer commentary. 1615 L was built in 1984 and renovated in 2018. Carr purchased it in 2016 for $229M , assuming a two-piece $134M CMBS loan. It housed Carr’s headquarters there until Carr moved into its Midtown Center development down the street this year. Carr failed to pay off its CMBS debt at maturity in September 2023, and a court appointed a receiver, Trigild, in July 2024. The property’s valuation has dipped drastically over the past 13 years. At the time of its securitization in 2013, 1615 L was appraised at $213M. But that number dropped to $51M as of last October, according to Morningstar Credit’s database. Trigild selected Cushman & Wakefield to lease the office space in July 2025, court documents show. At the time, the brokerage said it had 300K SF available , more than 200K SF of which was contiguous. Over the last year , Jemal Equities has purchased at least four other office buildings in D.C. proper. Last month, it paid $92.3M for a BXP office building on Connecticut Avenue anchored by Steptoe. That came after its May purchase of a Navy Yard office building for $93M. The firm this week launched its website, which lists not just office but also retail, hotel and multifamily holdings. Conversely, Carr has been quickly shedding office assets in the city over the past 18 months while shifting to focus on multifamily development . In mid-2025, it handed over three of its D.C. assets to a J.P. Morgan Asset Management fund as part of an equity buyout, Bisnow first reported at the time. Around the same time, it sold at least two other D.C.-area office buildings: 4500 East-West Highway in Bethesda and 901 K St. NW in the District.
